title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Page 116 finishes §XXXV. Euler calls the increment of ∫Z dx under arbitrary infinitesimal changes δy of the ordinates the 'variatio differentialis'. It is taken over 0 ≤ x ≤ a and normalised so that it vanishes at x = 0. Setting it equal to zero gives the maximum or minimum. He fixes the notation p = y', q = y'', r = y''', s = y'''' and so on.

Problem I: let Z = Z(x, y, p, q, r, s, ...) with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + ... Find the first variation of J = ∫_0^a Z dx.

Solution, step by step:
1. Since δx = 0, δJ = ∫δZ dx with δZ = N δy + P δp + Q δq + ...
2. Take dx constant. Because d and δ commute (§XXXII), δp = (δy)', δq = (δy)'', and so on.
3. Apply repeated integration by parts using the formulae of §XXXIV.
4. This gives δJ = ∫_0^a δy [N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − ...] dx, plus endpoint terms: δy(P − Q' + R'' − S''' + ...) + (δy)'(Q − R' + S'' − ...) + (δy)''(R − S' + ...) + (δy)'''(S − ...).

The integral part collects all the interior variations. In the remaining 'absolute' parts one sets x = a. There δy is the increment of the end ordinate, while dδy, ddδy, ... also depend on neighbouring ordinates.

The next page draws the consequences:
- the Euler–Poisson equation N − dP/dx + ddQ/dx² − ... = 0;
- an arbitrary constant for each integration, so extra conditions can be imposed;
- 'maximum maximorum' (free-end, i.e. natural) boundary conditions at x = a, and likewise at x = 0, since the constant of integration is chosen to make the variation vanish there.

In modern terms this is the first-variation formula, with boundary terms, for a higher-order Lagrangian in the δ-calculus.
errors: In the printed integration-by-parts line for the S-term, the final integral appears with a minus sign: −∫(δy/dx³) d⁴S. Four integrations by parts give +∫(δy/dx³) d⁴S. The collected result correctly has +d⁴S/dx⁴, so this is a typographical sign slip (if the scan is read correctly), not an error in the result.

Minor conceptual looseness: the lower limit is handled by choosing the integration constant so the variation vanishes at x = 0, rather than by evaluating the boundary terms between limits. This is equivalent, and Euler draws the correct conditions at x = 0 in Coroll. 4.

ideas.what: First variation of ∫Z(x, y, y', ..., y^(n)) dx via δ-operator commutation and repeated integration by parts
ideas.modern_name: First variation formula / Euler–Poisson (Euler–Lagrange) equation for higher-order Lagrangians
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi 1744, by geometric method); Lagrange 1760 (δ-method); Poisson for the name of the higher-order equation
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744); E296 Elementa calculi variationum and E297 (both Novi Comm. Petrop. 10, 1766)

ideas.what: Explicit boundary terms δy(P − Q' + R'' − ...) + δy'(Q − R' + ...) + ...
ideas.modern_name: Boundary terms of the first variation; natural boundary conditions
ideas.where_published: E297 itself, discussed in Goldstine's History of the Calculus of Variations and Opera omnia I.25

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-documented derivation of the Euler–Poisson equation with its boundary terms, in Euler's 1766 reformulation of Lagrange's δ-method. It is extensively covered in the histories of the calculus of variations.
transcription_corrections: 'quae oritur [?]' probably reads 'quae ita' (… 'quae ita intelligenda est').
In the S-line, check the sign of the last integral. The print appears to show '−∫ δy/dx³ d⁴S'; mathematically it should be '+'.
In δZ, the last term is S d⁴δy/dx⁴ (consistent with the transcription).
